newsitem.title: UK: Reeling pound unlikely to get boost from rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Reeling pound unlikely to get boost from rate rise.

text.p: Sterling's stumble to near five-month lows below $1.60 and its four-pfennig dive below 3.02 marks on Wednesday is unlikely to be reversed even if the Bank of England raises interest rates this week, said analysts.

"Paradoxically, a rate rise might actually be negative...A move to seven percent in base rates would probably be the last increase that we see for a few months," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
With expectations of more rate rises quelled, sterling - which has gained from this premise - would suffer.

"A rate hike tomorrow would certainly see a scale- back of expectations for the next Bank of England meeting in September...We would have seen four consecutive rate hikes and that would be time for the BoE to take a breather," said Duncan Frost from Bank Brussels Lambert sales department.

Sterling on Wednesday skidded in nervous European dealings as market sentiment shifted in favour of the BoE leaving rates unchanged at 6.75 percent after its two-day policy meeting which ends on Thursday.
The Bank is due to announce its rates decision at 1100 GMT on Thursday

"I think it is an extremely close call. But on balance, I still think a rate rise is likely though market expectations are shifting away from perceptions of a rate rise," said Adam Cole, economist at HSBC James Capel.
A Reuter poll said 16 out of 23 economists surveyed expected rates to rise from current 6.75 percent to 7.0 percent - the fourth-quarter point increase since May.

At 1100 GMT, sterling/mark was trading at 3.0180/90 against 3.0545/56 in late Europe on Tuesday and just off session troughs of 3.0095. Cable (sterling/dollar) was trading at $1.5972/82 against $1.6262/72 in late dealings though off session lows of $1.5918.

Traders said the stuffing was knocked out of sterling after an initial bout of profit-taking on cable, sparked by U.S. and Asian names, pushed the pair through stops around key support of $1.62 - dragging sterling/mark in its wake.
A powering dollar/mark, which scaled to near eight-year peaks of 1.8876, also weighed on the already bruised sterling.
And some analysts said investors were seen pulling out of sterling to put their money into the dollar.
"The dollar is taking over from sterling as the world's favourite investment currency," said Brian Martin, chief economist FX at BZW.
Flows out of sterling, said some, would not be reversed if the BoE hiked rates, but could be arrested.
"Now we have had this significant fall...maybe we could see a little support for the pound, " said BBL's Frost.
CIBC's Coleman said sterling could test 3.0 marks. "And if we did drop below 3.0 we might not see the highs of 3.05/3.06 marks again," he added.
Traders said once sterling pierced the $1.62 area on Wednesday, sell stops were triggered.

"People are perhaps hedging their bets for no-change in the BoE's monetary policy committee...People are getting panicky and jumping on the bandwagon while it is moving," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston.

Traders said there is mounting concern in markets at the the general strength of sterling, which scaled to 3.0878 marks and its highest since August 1989 in late July, as it chokes off exports and threatens unemployment.
Sterling's trade-weighed index stood at 104.5 compared to its close of 105.7 on Tuesday.
